newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian may displease IMF to pay pensions -dep PM.
newsitem.headline: Russian may displease IMF to pay pensions -dep PM.

text.p: Russia may have to run the risk of displeasing its international creditors in order to pay millions of dollars in overdue pensions, a top minister said on Thursday.

"The situation with debts for pensions is so serious that it seems we may have to go ahead with a decision that might not please certain international monetary organisations," First Deputy Prime Minister Viktor Ilyushin said.
"In principle, it's all the same to destitute pensioners whether inflation is one percent or three percent," he told the Federation Council upper house of parliament.

Ilyushin, however, made no comment on a call by the speaker of the Council, consisting of leaders of Russia's 89 regions, to allow the central bank to print more money if necessary. That would be anathema to international monetary officials.
Representatives of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) arrive in Moscow on Thursday for talks on paying out the latest delayed tranche of a $10 billion three-year loan.
The government and IMF say problems raising taxes have left the state with big debts.

The government has succeeded in bringing monthly inflation down to 1.2 percent a month in October. The annual increase in consumer prices slowed to a record low 27.2 percent in the year to October from 31.7 percent in the year to September.
But part of the cost of that austerity has been a failure to make budgeted payments to pensioners and state employees.

The head of the state pension fund, Vasily Barchuk, told the same Federation Council session the fund's debts to pensioners now stood at 15.7 trillion roubles and could exceed 20 trillion by the end of the year.
State sector wage arrears rose in October to 7.87 trillion roubles from 7.01 trillion.
Council speaker Igor Stroyev said the upper house would press, if necessary, for the central bank to issue more money -- a call that won support from many of the regional governors.
The Council voted to call on the government to take any measures that would allow it to pay its pension debts in full by December 1.
